title: Redesigning insect flight
doc_title: 15. Redesigning insect flight: the design space
home_blurb: The four-winged fly is famous. What nobody measured is whether it flies.
nothing_attempted_note: nothing here was run in an animal.
studies_note: Three studies, all simulations. None is an observation, none is calibrated to a measured four-winged fly, and nothing here was run in an animal. In the venation study two of four declared controls FAIL and are reported as failing rather than repaired, so read its controls before its result.
goal: Ultrabithorax represses wing identity on the third thoracic segment, and losing it gives Lewis's four-winged fly — one of the best-evidenced regulatory lesions in biology. The obvious engineering question is whether more wings means more flight. This page maps every route we can source to a redesigned flight apparatus, and asks what the four-winged fly would actually do if you threw it in the air.
summary: The famous mutant is famous for its appearance. We could find no published measurement of free flight in a four-winged Drosophila, so the question has an answer in the literature only if you assemble it from two separate phenotypes. Doing that, and then modelling the aerodynamics and the control loop, gives a worse outcome than the picture suggests — and for a reason that has nothing to do with wing number.

answer.headline: It would fly badly, for two reasons, and neither is "four wings".
paragraphs: Start with the result that needs no biology at all. Lift scales with the second moment of wing area, so splitting one wing into two smaller ones at the same total area and aspect ratio loses more than half of it. In our blade-element model, four wings at the same total area carry 0.46 body weights — it does not leave the ground. Four wings at double the area do fly, at 1.83 body weights, but they cost twice the mass-specific mechanical power. That kills the intuitive "redistribute the area" design before any gene is named, and it falls out of geometry.

The configuration the literature actually produced is worse than either, and the reason is the first thing a designer should know. In flies homozygous for the classic allele combination, the adults have two pairs of wings, but — in the authors' own words — "the homeotically transformed T3 (HT3) has only rudimentary indirect flight muscles". The lesion transforms the epidermis; the mesoderm keeps expressing Antennapedia, which is the likely reason the flight muscle never forms. You get a wing with no engine. Modelled, that configuration carries 0.84 body weights, and it stays below one at every non-negative value of the contested fore–hind interference term, so the conclusion does not rest on choosing a convenient value for a number nobody has pinned down.

The second cost is the sensor. A haltere is a hindwing already spent on something else — a gyroscopic rate sensor — and converting it back to a wing deletes it. The model says why that matters, and the useful form of the answer is not "vision is weaker". Sweeping the feedback delay and giving every delay the best gain available to it, no loop slower than about three wingbeats, 14 milliseconds, can meet the measured recovery from a disturbance at any gain. The haltere loop is inside that bound. The visual loop is well outside it. Vision is not too weak; it is too slow to be turned up.

A caution the page insists on: none of this says four wings are worse than two. Dragonflies have flown with four independently controlled wings for 300 million years, and their fore–hind phasing can improve efficiency rather than cost it. Remove roughly half the wing area from a moth or a butterfly and it still flies, losing acceleration but not turning radius. What makes the dipteran case different is specific to Diptera: the hindwing has already been spent, so converting it back costs a sensor and arrives without an engine.

So the route worth proposing is the one nobody has run. Transform the T3 mesoderm as well as the epidermis, and give the second wing pair an engine. Both halves are published separately — that T2 mesoderm is specified entirely by induction and expresses no selector of its own, that ectopic homeotic expression in it respecifies its muscle, and that Antennapedia persists in the transformed T3 mesoderm. The experiment is to run that in the other direction.
answer.precision_note: We found no published measurement of free-flight performance in a four-winged Drosophila. Everything above assembles two separately published phenotypes — rudimentary indirect flight muscle in the transformed segment, and haltere necessity in otherwise normal flies — plus our own model. Nobody has thrown one in the air and measured it.

chain.title: The chain across scales, and where it is not calibrated
chain.intro: From a Hox dose to a body in the air. One junction is a model whose held-out prediction lands, one is a published phenotype, one is refused, and one is a null.

links.note: The best-supported junction here. Calibrated on the Ubx arm alone, the model predicts the independently measured Antennapedia threshold to within 4.0%, against 39.2% for the switch-like variant — and both variants pass the same controls, so it is a fair comparison rather than a strawman. Stronger still, a test that needs no model: the two published thresholds sit on opposite branches of the switch, and their ordering is the one a hysteretic switch forbids.

Refused, and this is the design space's central finding. Epidermal identity follows the lesion; mesodermal identity does not, so the transformed segment gets a wing and no indirect flight muscle. The two are controlled separately and nobody has transformed both. Until someone does, 'four-winged fly' names an animal with two wings and two ornaments.

Inside the blade-element model, and the part of it that matters is geometric rather than biological: lift goes with the second moment of wing area. Same total area over four wings gives 0.46 body weights; double area gives 1.83 at twice the power. 18 of its 24 parameters are assumed, so the ratios are more trustworthy than the absolute numbers, and the model is calibrated so that wild type supports exactly body weight.

A delay bound rather than a gain comparison: no loop slower than about three wingbeats meets the measured recovery at any gain in the declared family. The model recovers in 13 ms where the real fly takes under 60, so it is OPTIMISTIC about control and therefore understates the cost of deleting the sensor.

A genuine null, reported because it is the story one would otherwise tell. Four-wing recovery curves sit within 1% of two-wing ones at a 0.5% wing-mass fraction. The four-winged fly's control problem is the deleted sensor, not the added rotational inertia.

chain.verdict: The end-to-end statement — this allele gives that flight performance — is refused, because the animal it describes has never been flown. What the chain does deliver is an ordering of the obstacles: the missing engine comes first, the missing sensor second, and the added inertia not at all.

not_claimed: No fly was made, no animal was used, and no wet-lab experiment was run for this page.
There is no published measurement of free-flight performance in a four-winged Drosophila. The conclusion assembles two separately published phenotypes plus our own model.

This page does not claim that four wings are worse than two. Odonata and the hindwing-ablation literature refute that as a general statement; the claim here is specific to Diptera, where the hindwing has already been spent on a sensor.

The venation study fails two of its four declared controls, including the one added to ask whether its readout had converged. Part of its quoted seed spread is convergence rather than pattern formation, and the runs were not lengthened until it passed.
18 of the flight model's 24 parameters are assumed rather than sourced. Its ratios are more trustworthy than its absolute numbers.
A threshold in a model is not a threshold in an animal.

closing.title: What this page is for

link.text: The working notes, including the sentence this page must not write

closing.text: The four-winged fly has been a textbook picture for fifty years, and the picture is of an appearance. Asking what it would do in the air turns one famous lesion into an ordered list of obstacles, two of which are published and separate and one of which is a null. Every route here carries its evidence level, a row read only at listing level says so rather than being paraphrased, and two of the controls on this page failed and say so. The useful output is not the answer but the next experiment: give the second pair an engine.

schematic.intro: One thorax, three segments, and the two things the famous lesion does not change. The routes below act at different places in this picture, and the reason the four-winged fly flies badly is that two of these places are controlled separately.
schematic.title: Where each family of routes acts on the thorax of a fly
schematic.desc: On the left, a fly's thorax in side view with its three segments labelled T1, T2 and T3. T2 carries a wing above and an indirect flight muscle inside it; T3 carries a haltere, a small club-shaped organ, above a segment whose interior is drawn empty to show it has only rudimentary flight muscle. An arrow marks the homeotic transformation that converts the T3 haltere into a second wing while leaving the muscle compartment empty. On the right, two small panels: above, a wing outline with its longitudinal veins and a bracket showing the model makes one vein too few; below, a feedback diagram in which a haltere feeds a fast loop and an eye feeds a slow one into the same wing-steering output, with a delay bound marked at three wingbeats. Six numbered pins mark where the routes act; each is named in the list under the figure.
schematic.caption: Schematic, not a measurement and not to scale.

pins.name: The Ubx switch and its enhancers
pins.note: Where appendage identity is decided, and the resolution at which this is a design problem rather than a knockout. Hox dose rather than Hox presence sets the outcome, and our model's held-out prediction lands within 4% on the graded reading.

pins.name: Wing specification in T2
pins.note: vestigial, scalloped, apterous, nubbin — the selectors that make a wing a wing. Repressing them is how T3 is kept a haltere, and de-repressing them is how the famous mutant gets its second pair.

pins.name: The indirect flight muscle
pins.note: The engine, and the reason the four-winged fly is a disappointment. Mesodermal identity is controlled separately from epidermal identity, so the transformed segment gets a wing and only rudimentary muscle. This is the route the page recommends fixing.

pins.name: The transformation itself
pins.note: What the classic allele combination actually does: it converts the T3 epidermis, leaving the mesoderm expressing Antennapedia. A wing arrives; an engine does not.

pins.name: Vein patterning
pins.note: Lateral inhibition sets vein spacing on the blade. Our model gets the spacing right to 0.07% of linear theory and the count wrong by a near-constant one vein — a boundary effect, not a scaling error. Two of its four controls fail.

pins.name: The haltere and the control loop
pins.note: A hindwing already spent on a gyroscopic rate sensor. Converting it back deletes it, and no loop slower than about three wingbeats can meet the measured recovery at any gain — so vision cannot simply be turned up to compensate.
